title: Subvert Trust Controls
summary: Subvert Trust Controls covers the family of behaviours that weaken or remove the signals an operating system uses to decide whether code, a driver or a website deserves trust. These signals are the ones a user actually sees: a signature that validates, a warning that a file came from the internet, a browser refusal to continue to an unknown certificate authority. An adversary can attack the check rather than the code, by altering the settings that store trust decisions, changing the permissions on the artefacts those checks rely on, injecting a certificate into the trust store, or signing the payload with a stolen or fraudulently issued certificate so that the check passes honestly. The technique is a parent category, so the telemetry varies by child, but the common thread is a change to trust configuration rather than a change to the malicious file itself, and that configuration change is what a defender should watch.

beginner.definition: Computers use trust checks to warn you before running unknown software or opening an unsafe website. This technique is when an attacker changes those checks. Instead of breaking the lock, they change the rule about which keys count as valid.
beginner.whyItMatters: These warnings are your last chance to stop something harmful. If an attacker can silence them, harmful files look normal. Users then run the file without hesitation. Antivirus and application rules may also be fooled, so the whole defence layer weakens at once.
howItWorks: The system keeps trust information, such as certificates and trust settings, in stores and files.
It checks that information before it runs code or opens a secure website.
The attacker changes a trust setting or adds a certificate they control.
The same check now passes for content it should have blocked or flagged.
The user sees no warning at all, so the harmful program runs quietly.
The attacker then repeats the changes on other hosts to keep access.
beginner.example: Imagine an airport where staff check passports at the gate. A traveller cannot fake the airline's stamp, so instead they change the book of approved stamps kept at the desk. From then on, any document they carry is waved through, and the guard believes the check was done properly. Subverting trust controls is the same idea: the guard still works, but the rules were quietly rewritten.
takeaways: Trust settings and certificate stores are configuration, so monitor changes to them.
A file with a valid signature is not automatically safe if the signing key was stolen.
Users need to report unexpected security warnings instead of clicking past them.

objectives: Explain what operating system trust controls are and what they protect against.
Describe the main ways an adversary can weaken or bypass a trust check.
Identify the configuration locations and artefacts that trust decisions depend on.
Explain why valid signatures alone do not prove that a file is safe.
List monitoring approaches that reveal changes to trust settings and certificate stores.
